subject: Lighting and power for productive work
hook: Plan the sockets before you choose the desk.
ig:
Most home office problems are power problems: too few sockets, a lamp in the wrong place and a nest of cables under the desk.

The new year is when a lot of people finally sort the spare room or box room into a proper place to work. Before anyone draws a desk, these five things decide whether it works day to day:

1. Count the plugs you actually use, then add one.
2. Mark every socket and switch so the furniture never blocks them.
3. Put the screen side-on to the window to cut glare.
4. Place a task light on the side of your non-writing hand.
5. Plan a cable route: grommet, tray, hidden drop.

One honest note: new sockets or light circuits are a job for a qualified electrician. Our part is planning the fitted home office furniture around them, so the cut-outs, grommets and cable routes are made in the workshop, not improvised on the day.

Save this for when you plan your desk, and tap the link in bio to book a free, no-obligation design consultation.
fb:
Back to work this week? If your desk is still the kitchen table or a corner with an extension lead trailing across the floor, this one is for you.

We've put together the five power and lighting checks we go through before designing any fitted desk: how many plugs you really need, where the sockets sit, which way the screen should face, where a task light goes and how the cables get from desk to wall without being seen.

If you need extra sockets, get a qualified electrician in first. We'll show you where they'll be most useful once the furniture is designed.

on_asset: S1: Plan the sockets before the desk | 5 checks for a desk that works | S2: Count every plug — List each device: monitor, laptop, lamp, phone charger, printer, router. Most home offices need more than one double socket, so plan it now rather than with an extension lead. | S3: Note where sockets sit — A desk carcass or upstand can cover a socket. Every socket and switch is recorded at survey so panels get a cut-out or an access point in the right place. | S4: Turn the screen side-on — Set the screen at right angles to the window. You cut glare on the monitor and avoid sitting as a dark silhouette on video calls. | S5: Light the task, not the room — A ceiling light behind you throws your shadow on the desk. Plan a lamp spot on the side of your non-writing hand, or a light point under a shelf. | S6: Give every cable a route — Grommet holes, a tray under the worktop and a hidden drop behind a side panel keep leads off the floor and away from feet. | S7: Save this before you plan | Sockets counted, screen side-on, task light placed, cables routed.
